snapshots.name: Monnica
snapshots.body: Augustine's mother, a devout Christian whose prayers and tears for her son's conversion run through the whole book. Her steady faith stands in deliberate contrast to her son's long years of searching.

snapshots.name: Patricius
snapshots.body: Augustine's father, a man of modest means who works hard to fund his son's education, though he does not share his wife's faith until near the end of his life. His temper and his ambitions for Augustine shape the household of Augustine's childhood.

snapshots.name: Ambrose
snapshots.body: The bishop of Milan, renowned as a preacher, whose sermons Augustine begins attending at first only to study his rhetorical technique. His preaching gradually opens for Augustine a way of reading scripture he had not considered possible.

snapshots.name: Alypius
snapshots.body: A close friend of Augustine from their shared hometown, who follows him through many of the same intellectual and spiritual turns. His own struggle with a taste for the arena's violence is one of the book's memorable digressions.

snapshots.name: Nebridius
snapshots.body: A friend of Augustine who shares in his restless philosophical questioning during the years in Carthage and Milan. Their conversations are among those Augustine recalls as most engaged with the deep problems that trouble him.

snapshots.name: Faustus
snapshots.body: A celebrated bishop of the Manichees whose arrival Augustine had long anticipated, hoping he could resolve the doubts building up about the sect's teachings. The meeting proves a turning point in Augustine's disillusionment with Manichaeism.

snapshots.name: Adeodatus
snapshots.body: Augustine's son, born to him in his youth outside of marriage. He grows up alongside his father's long spiritual searching.

snapshots.name: Victorinus
snapshots.body: A celebrated Roman rhetorician and philosopher whose late-life conversion to Christianity is recounted to Augustine by Simplicianus. His willingness to make his faith public, despite his standing, deeply affects Augustine.

snapshots.name: Pontitianus
snapshots.body: A fellow African serving at the imperial court, who visits Augustine and Alypius and tells them the story of two officials converted by reading about the monk Antony. His account is the immediate spark for the book's climactic garden scene.

snapshots.name: Antony
snapshots.body: An Egyptian monk celebrated for abandoning his possessions to live a life of ascetic devotion in the desert. The story of his sudden conversion, retold to Augustine by Pontitianus, strikes Augustine with particular force.

snapshots.name: Cicero
snapshots.body: The Roman orator and philosopher whose now-lost work Hortensius first awakened in the young Augustine a love of wisdom for its own sake. Augustine credits this early reading with redirecting his ambitions, even before he had any interest in Christianity.

snapshots.name: Simplicianus
snapshots.body: An elder priest in Milan, later Ambrose's successor as bishop, whom Augustine seeks out to discuss his reading of scripture and philosophy. It is Simplicianus who tells him the story of Victorinus's conversion.

snapshots.name: Verecundus
snapshots.body: A friend who lends Augustine and his companions the use of his country house at Cassiciacum after Augustine's decision to leave his teaching post. His own hesitation about converting weighs on him even as he helps his friends.

snapshots.name: Romanianus
snapshots.body: A wealthy patron from Augustine's hometown who supported his education and later his teaching career. Augustine remains grateful to him even as their paths diverge over the years.

snapshots.name: Manichees
snapshots.body: A religious sect, blending Christian language with a strict dualism of light and dark, that Augustine follows for nearly a decade during his twenties. His growing dissatisfaction with their teachings, culminating in the disappointing meeting with Faustus, drives much of the book's middle books.
